name: Hazari
description: Hazari (meaning 'One Thousand') is a highly strategic partitioning game popular in Bangladesh and Bhutan. Players receive 13 cards and must divide them into four sets (composed of 3, 3, 3, and 4 cards). These sets are then compared against opponents' sets in a fixed order. The game combines the hand-ranking logic of Brag and Teen Patti with a unique structural challenge and a long-term scoring goal of 1000 points.

history.origins: Originating in South Asia, Hazari is closely related to the British game 'Crash' (or Thirteen-card Brag). It has become the most popular card game in Bangladesh, often played in tea stalls and social clubs.
timeline: Mid-20th Century: Hazari evolves from 13-card Brag variants in colonial Bengal.
1971-Present: Becomes a cultural staple in independent Bangladesh.
Modern Era: Digital versions thrive among the Bangladeshi diaspora.
history.cultural: Typically played with a distinct Bangladeshi fervor, often involves 'calling' your sets loudly when ready.
history.evolution: The game standardized the 10-point value for all high cards (10 through Ace), simplifying the mental math of its 1000-point target.

setup.dealing: Dealer deals 13 cards to each player in batches (e.g., 4-4-5 or all at once).

rules.objective: Be the first player to reach a cumulative score of 1000 points by winning card comparisons.
rules.gameplay:
1. PARTITIONING: Each player arranges their 13 cards into four sets. Three sets contain 3 cards each, and the fourth (final) set contains 4 cards. Players must arrange them so they are played from strongest to weakest (though this is a strategy, not a restriction).
2. CALLING: When all players have partitioned their cards, they call 'Up' or 'Ready'.
3. COMPARISONS: There are four rounds of comparison. In each, players reveal one set. The winner of a comparison takes all cards from that round. The winner of Comparison 1 leads Comparison 2, and so on.
4. POINT SCORING: High cards (A, K, Q, J, 10) are worth 10 points each. Other cards (2-9) are worth 0 points.
keyRules: Ranking of 3rd-card sets (highest to lowest): 1. Troy (Three of a Kind), 2. Color Run (Straight Flush), 3. Run (Straight), 4. Color (Flush), 5. Pair, 6. High Card.
Total points in the deck are 200.
If sets are equal in rank, the highest card within the set determines the winner.

strategy.basic: Try to win at least two comparisons. Don't put all your high cards in one set if you can split them to win two tricks.
strategy.intermediate: If you have an Ace, King, and 10 of different suits, they may be better used as high cards in a 'Color' or 'Run' than as individual point cards in a weak set.
strategy.advanced: Defensive Partitioning: If you have a mediocre hand, try to win the 'fourth' set (the 4-card set) as it often contains more point cards dumped by others who won early with Troys.
tips: A 'Troy' of Aces is the strongest possible set.
A 'Color Run' of A-K-Q is nearly unbeatable.
Count how many 10-point cards have been taken to know what is left in the final set.

synthesis.shortDescription: A tactical partitioning game from Bangladesh where you divide 13 cards into four sets. Out-rank your opponents in head-to-head comparisons to capture high-value cards and reach 1000 points.
